paper.title: Live longer, work longer? An investigation of the health capacity to work at older ages in Denmark using combined register and survey data
paper.code_data_availability: Availability of the data and materials: “Due to Danish Data Protection Legislation, only Danish research environments can be granted authorisation to Danish administrative registers. …

registers.name_in_paper: the comprehensive Danish register data from Statistics Denmark (‘the Danish registers’)
registers.role: outcome (labour market attachment), treatment components (register-based health indicators), controls, linkage, sample frame
variables_mentioned: healthcare utilisation (prescription drugs; GP, psychologist, psychiatrist, chiropractor and physiotherapist visits; somatic and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient admissions)

registers.name_in_paper: Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), Danish part, waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6
registers.role: treatment components (survey health indicators not available in the registers); sample frame
variables_mentioned: quality of life measured by CASP
latest-held occupation (for a small number of respondents)

linkages: Danish part of SHARE linked to longitudinal Danish administrative register data from Statistics Denmark at the individual level (3,761 unique individuals, 14,502 year observations before exclusions); the personal identification number is named as a key linkage variable

sample.universe: Individuals aged 50–79 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6) who can be linked to the Danish administrative registers
selection_rules: start from the Danish part of SHARE waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004, 2006/2007, 2011, 2013, 2015) that can be linked to the Danish registers: 3,761 unique individuals / 14,502 year observations
exclude individuals younger than 50 years and older than 79 years
exclude those with missing information on key variables, including the personal identification number (exclusions listed in Additional file 1: Table S2)
final sample: 1,521 men (3,627 year observations) and 1,638 women (3,849 year observations)
96 year observations missing self-employed/employee status are additionally excluded from the self-employment analyses
stage-one employment regressions are run on the 50–54 age group only; stage two predicts for ages 55 and above
sample.n_observations: 3,627 year observations for men and 3,849 for women (7,476 in total); 14,502 linked year observations before exclusions
sample.n_individuals: 1,521 men and 1,638 women (3,761 unique linked individuals before exclusions)

construction_notes: Health indices: first principal component of the health indicators (Poterba et al. 2013), converted into a percentile score per individual; a higher percentile score indicates better health. All loadings are positive for the base case index, i.e. higher values of the raw first principal component represent poorer health.

Base case index uses 56 health indicators; the mental index uses mental disorders, psychologist/psychiatrist visits and psychiatric inpatient/outpatient admissions; the physical index uses smoking, BMI, physical and mobility limitations, somatic diagnoses, chiropractor/physiotherapist visits and somatic inpatient/outpatient visits. Self-assessed health, quality of life, GP visits and comorbidities are excluded from the two split indices.
Mean base-case health percentile: men aged 50–54 = 64.7, women aged 50–54 = 55.4; men aged 75–79 = 38.2, women aged 75–79 = 34.4.
Education: highest achieved education expressed as education quartiles defined within year of birth and gender, to account for rising educational attainment (Bound et al. 2015).
Occupation: current or latest-held occupation coded to ISCO-08 and aggregated into four groups — white-collar (ISCO 1–3), pink-collar (ISCO 4–5), blue-collar (ISCO 6–8) and low-skilled (ISCO 9).

Chronic illnesses: eight illnesses identified with the Danish Health Data Authority algorithm from hospital contact or prescription within the 10 years before interview; 31 physical and psychiatric diagnoses within 10 years prior to interview; Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index over a ten-year period; healthcare utilisation in the year preceding the interview.
Additional work capacity = predicted (counterfactual) employment rate from Eq. (2) minus the actual employment rate of the age group.

claims.statement: Among Danes aged 50–54, a higher base case health index (better health) is associated with a higher probability of being employed for men, in a linear probability model with covariates.

treatment.label: Base case health index

definition.value: Base case health index: the first principal component of 56 health indicators, converted into a percentile score (0–100) where a higher score indicates better health. Indicators include self-assessed health, quality of life (CASP), functional and physical limitations, low grip strength, 31 diagnoses, prescription-drug use, primary and secondary healthcare utilisation, eight chronic illnesses and the Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index. Built from the Danish part of SHARE linked to Danish administrative registers.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview wave, contemporaneously with employment, at ages 50–54. Diagnoses and chronic illnesses are taken over the 10 years before the interview and healthcare utilisation in the year preceding it.

outcome.label: Employed (binary indicator of being employed)

definition.value: E_i, a binary variable indicating whether the individual is employed or not, taken from the register measure of labour market attachment, which is measured annually. Entered as the dependent variable of a linear probability model.

timing.value: Same observation year as the health index, at ages 50–54.

units.value: change in the probability of being employed per one-percentile-point increase in the health index (linear probability model; the index runs from 0 to 100)

magnitude.interpretation: A ten-percentage point increase in the base case health index (e.g. being at the 70th rather than the 60th percentile of health) raises the likelihood of working by 4.9 percentage points for men.

estimand.target_population: Danes aged 50–54 observed in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6) and linked to the Danish administrative registers, men only
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: health and employment are measured in the same observation year
estimand.formal_query: E[Employed | do(health index = h+1), X] − E[Employed | do(health index = h), X] for Danish men aged 50–54

population.description: Danes aged 50–54 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, collected 2004–2015) linked to the Danish administrative registers; estimated separately by gender
subgroups_defined: education quartile (by birth year and gender)
population.selection: Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) respondents who could be linked to the Danish administrative registers; aged 50–79 with non-missing key variables including the personal identification number. The authors note that respondents in SHARE are more socio-economically advantaged than the general population.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in the health index among 50–54-year-olds, an age window chosen because their employment decision is not influenced by the availability of early retirement. There is no reform, instrument or discontinuity: identification rests on the covariate set.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on education, marital status, being born in Denmark, area of residence and survey wave, the health index is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of employment, so that beta_1 recovers the effect of health on employment rather than a spurious association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No balance test, no instrument and no placebo are reported; the covariate list is given in the Fig. 2 caption and under Eq. (1). The authors describe beta_1 both as an 'effect' and as an 'association'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Employment / retirement does not cause the measured health index (no reverse causality).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors explicitly concede they cannot rule it out and say that if retirement improves health they overestimate the ability to work given health.

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the estimation sample to ages 50–54 removes non-health-related retirement, because employment decisions at those ages are not influenced by the availability of early retirement; otherwise the estimated effect of health would be biased downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text; supported by a robustness check that re-estimates on 55–59-year-olds and finds no notable differences.

implies_edges.to: inclusion in the stage-one estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Justification bias in the self-reported components of the health index is limited, i.e. non-working individuals do not systematically report worse health.
key_assumptions.supported_by: A robustness check recomputing the health index from objective (register-based) measures only, which gives similar results for additional work capacity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in the health index is not systematically related to socio-economic status (lower socio-economic groups are not simply diagnosed later or seen less often by the health system).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing; raised in the discussion as a reason the ability to work of lower socio-economic groups would be overestimated.

threats_discussed: reverse causality: retirement may improve health, so the health–employment gradient may be overstated
justification bias in self-reported health (Bound 1991): non-working individuals may report worse health
systematic differences in measurement error across socio-economic groups (Bago d’Uva et al. 2008)
lower socio-economic groups may use less healthcare and be diagnosed later, overestimating their ability to work
SHARE respondents are more socio-economically advantaged than the general population
late-onset, age-related conditions such as dementia are not appropriately captured by the model
occupational selection bias in the self-employed/employee comparison
health may be endogenous to years of work (wearing out)
robustness_checks: re-estimating the employment regressions on 55–59-year-olds instead of 50–54-year-olds
excluding education as a covariate
estimating with the health index and time dummies as the only covariates
predicting women’s health capacity to work using the male regression coefficients
a health index computed separately for men and women
including the change in health indices between waves as an additional covariate
a health index based solely on objective (not self-assessed) measures, to address justification bias
unresolved_confounders: reverse causality from retirement to health
systematic differences in measurement error across socio-economic groups
later diagnosis / lower healthcare use among individuals with lower socio-economic position
age-related late-onset conditions (e.g. dementia) not captured by the health index

estimator.value: OLS linear probability model with cluster-robust standard errors at the individual level, estimated separately for men and women

estimation.specification: Eq. (1): E_i^{50−54} = β0 + β1 H_i^{50−54} + β2 X_i^{50−54} + ε_i, one regression per health index and gender
controls: education (4 dummies, education quartiles by birth year and gender)

source_table.value: Figure 2 (coefficient plot), p. 7 — the 'Base case health index' row, men series

adjustment_set.label: education (quartiles by year of birth and gender, 4 dummies)

heterogeneity.finding: Re-estimated by educational attainment (Additional file 1: Figures S1, S2): an educational gradient in the magnitude of the association, with the smallest positive coefficient for the highly educated. For women in the 4th education quartile the mental and physical indices are not significant; for men the same goes for the mental health index.
Re-estimated by occupational group (Additional file 1: Figures S1, S2): an occupational gradient, with the smallest positive coefficient for those with white-collar jobs.

heterogeneity.dimension: health index (base case vs mental vs physical)
heterogeneity.finding: The mental health index has the smallest impact on employment, while physical health impacts more.
Regressions are run separately for men and women; the base case coefficient is 4.9 percentage points per ten percentile points for men and 5.0 for women.

edges.to: inclusion in the stage-one estimation sample

ambiguities: The paper prints no regression table: the coefficient is read off the Fig. 2 coefficient plot. Only the two base case values are anchored in the text (footnote 3).

The authors describe beta_1 both as 'the effect of health on employment' and as 'the association between health and employment'; the estimand is recorded as an ATE because the paper reasons about bias in 'the estimated effect of health on retirement', but the design is a covariate-adjusted cross-sectional regression.

Education is entered as a control while the paper also says 'education is likely to affect retirement both directly and indirectly through health', i.e. it may be a mediator; its role in the adjustment set is recorded as unclear.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 2 Employment regression coefficients for the different health indices by gender. The figure displays regression coefficients and their 95% confidence intervals (cluster robust standard errors). We regress a variable for being employed on each health index for the age group of 50–54-year-olds. Specifications include the covariates: Education (4 dummies), married (1 dummy), being born in Denmark (1 dummy), area of residence (4 dummies), and wave (5 dummies)

evidence.how: Equation (1) as typeset on page 4 of the PDF, transcribed character by character from the rendered formula; mathematical typesetting does not survive plain-text extraction, so it is recorded as a transcription rather than a quote.

Footnote 3 on page 6 states that a ten-percentage point increase in the base case health index raises the likelihood of working by 4.9 percentage points for men. Dividing by the ten percentile points of the stated increase gives the per-percentile-point coefficient 0.0049 plotted in Fig. 2; an independent pixel measurement of the Fig. 2 marker against the printed x-axis ticks (0.000 / 0.002 / 0.004 / 0.006) at 600 dpi returns 0.00486, which agrees.

Endpoints of the plotted 95% confidence interval for the men / Base case health index row of Fig. 2, measured in the same 600 dpi render against the same x-axis ticks: lower whisker 0.0038, upper whisker 0.0059. The paper prints no numeric interval; the reading is precise to roughly ±0.0002.

value.parameter_of_interest: β1

index_sets.over: individuals aged 50–54 in the linked SHARE–register sample

value.normalisation: H is the health index expressed as a percentile score (0–100) of the first principal component, a higher score meaning better health, so no omitted category applies to it; X contains education (4 dummies), married, born in Denmark, area of residence (4 dummies) and wave (5 dummies), each with an unnamed omitted category. Estimated separately for men and women.
value.link_function: identity (linear probability model)

treatment.label: Base case health index at ages 55–59, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Base case health index: the first principal component of 56 health indicators, converted into a percentile score (0–100) where a higher score indicates better health. Indicators include self-assessed health, quality of life (CASP), functional and physical limitations, low grip strength, 31 diagnoses, prescription-drug use, primary and secondary healthcare utilisation, eight chronic illnesses and the Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 55–59; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (base case health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

claims.statement: Danish men aged 70–74 have an estimated additional work capacity of an amount the figure does not let one read when health is measured by the base case health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. treatment.label: Base case health index at ages 70–74, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Base case health index: the first principal component of 56 health indicators, converted into a percentile score (0–100) where a higher score indicates better health. Indicators include self-assessed health, quality of life (CASP), functional and physical limitations, low grip strength, 31 diagnoses, prescription-drug use, primary and secondary healthcare utilisation, eight chronic illnesses and the Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index. Built from the Danish part of SHARE linked to Danish administrative registers. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 70–74; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (base case health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The base case health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

population.description: Danish men aged 70–74 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, collected 2004–2015) linked to the Danish administrative registers; the prediction uses coefficients estimated on 50–54-year-olds of the same gender

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. claims.statement: Danish men aged 55–59 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.04 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the mental health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Mental health index at ages 55–59, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Mental health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the mental-health subset of the indicators — mental disorders, visits to psychologists and psychiatrists, and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient admissions. Self-assessed health, quality of life, GP visits and comorbidities are excluded from the split indices because they contain elements of both types of health. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 55–59; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (mental health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The mental health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

estimand.target_population: Danish men aged 55–59 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6) linked to the Danish administrative registers
estimand.formal_query: E[Ê_i^a | age group a] − E[E_i | age group a], where Ê_i^a is the employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) using the 50–54 coefficients

population.description: Danish men aged 55–59 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, collected 2004–2015) linked to the Danish administrative registers; the prediction uses coefficients estimated on 50–54-year-olds of the same gender
population.selection: Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) respondents who could be linked to the Danish administrative registers; aged 50–79 with non-missing key variables including the personal identification number. The authors note that respondents in SHARE are more socio-economically advantaged than the general population.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. The two-stage Cutler, Meara and Richards-Shubik (2013) health-capacity-to-work method: a covariate-adjusted employment–health gradient estimated on 50–54-year-olds (an age window not yet eligible for early retirement) is applied out of sample to the observed health and characteristics of the older age group, and the gap between that counterfactual employment rate and the actual one is reported as additional work capacity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on education, marital status, being born in Denmark, area of residence and survey wave, the health index is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of employment, so that beta_1 recovers the effect of health on employment rather than a spurious association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No balance test, no instrument and no placebo are reported; the covariate list is given in the Fig. 2 caption and under Eq. (1). The authors describe beta_1 both as an 'effect' and as an 'association'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Employment / retirement does not cause the measured health index (no reverse causality).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors explicitly concede they cannot rule it out and say that if retirement improves health they overestimate the ability to work given health.

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the estimation sample to ages 50–54 removes non-health-related retirement, because employment decisions at those ages are not influenced by the availability of early retirement; otherwise the estimated effect of health would be biased downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text; supported by a robustness check that re-estimates on 55–59-year-olds and finds no notable differences.

implies_edges.to: inclusion in the stage-one estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Justification bias in the self-reported components of the health index is limited, i.e. non-working individuals do not systematically report worse health.
key_assumptions.supported_by: A robustness check recomputing the health index from objective (register-based) measures only, which gives similar results for additional work capacity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in the health index is not systematically related to socio-economic status (lower socio-economic groups are not simply diagnosed later or seen less often by the health system).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing; raised in the discussion as a reason the ability to work of lower socio-economic groups would be overestimated.

key_assumptions.assumption: The employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds also holds for the older age groups, so that applying beta_1^{50-54} to their health gives their counterfactual employment rate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussed as a limitation ('it is likely that health conditions have a smaller effect on employment for younger (50–54-year-olds) than for older cohorts'); supported by a robustness check re-estimating on 55–59-year-olds with no notable differences.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing; stated as an assumption whose failure would make health capacity to work overestimated.

key_assumptions.assumption: The health index captures the health conditions that determine the ability to work at older ages; late-onset, age-related conditions such as dementia are acknowledged not to be appropriately captured, which would bias the estimate upwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing; stated in the list of reasons the estimates are upper bounds.

claims.statement: Danish men aged 70–74 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.80 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the mental health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Mental health index at ages 70–74, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Mental health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the mental-health subset of the indicators — mental disorders, visits to psychologists and psychiatrists, and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient admissions. Self-assessed health, quality of life, GP visits and comorbidities are excluded from the split indices because they contain elements of both types of health. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 70–74; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (mental health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The mental health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

estimand.target_population: Danish men aged 70–74 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6) linked to the Danish administrative registers
estimand.formal_query: E[Ê_i^a | age group a] − E[E_i | age group a], where Ê_i^a is the employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) using the 50–54 coefficients

population.description: Danish men aged 70–74 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, collected 2004–2015) linked to the Danish administrative registers; the prediction uses coefficients estimated on 50–54-year-olds of the same gender

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. The two-stage Cutler, Meara and Richards-Shubik (2013) health-capacity-to-work method: a covariate-adjusted employment–health gradient estimated on 50–54-year-olds (an age window not yet eligible for early retirement) is applied out of sample to the observed health and characteristics of the older age group, and the gap between that counterfactual employment rate and the actual one is reported as additional work capacity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on education, marital status, being born in Denmark, area of residence and survey wave, the health index is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of employment, so that beta_1 recovers the effect of health on employment rather than a spurious association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No balance test, no instrument and no placebo are reported; the covariate list is given in the Fig. 2 caption and under Eq. (1). The authors describe beta_1 both as an 'effect' and as an 'association'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the estimation sample to ages 50–54 removes non-health-related retirement, because employment decisions at those ages are not influenced by the availability of early retirement; otherwise the estimated effect of health would be biased downwards.

definition.value: Physical health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the physical-health subset of the indicators — smoking, BMI, physical and mobility limitations, somatic diagnoses, visits to chiropractor and physiotherapist, and somatic inpatient and outpatient visits. treatment.label: Base case health index at ages 55–59, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Base case health index: the first principal component of 56 health indicators, converted into a percentile score (0–100) where a higher score indicates better health. Indicators include self-assessed health, quality of life (CASP), functional and physical limitations, low grip strength, 31 diagnoses, prescription-drug use, primary and secondary healthcare utilisation, eight chronic illnesses and the Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index. Built from the Danish part of SHARE linked to Danish administrative registers. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 55–59; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (base case health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. claims.statement: Danish women aged 70–74 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.73 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the base case health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Base case health index at ages 70–74, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Base case health index: the first principal component of 56 health indicators, converted into a percentile score (0–100) where a higher score indicates better health. Indicators include self-assessed health, quality of life (CASP), functional and physical limitations, low grip strength, 31 diagnoses, prescription-drug use, primary and secondary healthcare utilisation, eight chronic illnesses and the Elixhauser-van Walraven comorbidity index. Built from the Danish part of SHARE linked to Danish administrative registers. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 70–74; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (base case health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The base case health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

claims.statement: Danish women aged 55–59 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.06 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the mental health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Mental health index at ages 55–59, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Mental health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the mental-health subset of the indicators — mental disorders, visits to psychologists and psychiatrists, and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient admissions. Self-assessed health, quality of life, GP visits and comorbidities are excluded from the split indices because they contain elements of both types of health. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 55–59; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (mental health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The mental health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the estimation sample to ages 50–54 removes non-health-related retirement, because employment decisions at those ages are not influenced by the availability of early retirement; otherwise the estimated effect of health would be biased downwards.

claims.statement: Danish women aged 70–74 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.79 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the mental health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Mental health index at ages 70–74, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Mental health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the mental-health subset of the indicators — mental disorders, visits to psychologists and psychiatrists, and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient admissions. Self-assessed health, quality of life, GP visits and comorbidities are excluded from the split indices because they contain elements of both types of health. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 70–74; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (mental health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The mental health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

claims.statement: Danish women aged 70–74 have an estimated additional work capacity of 0.73 (share of the age group) when health is measured by the physical health index: given their health, the two-stage Cutler et al. (2013) method predicts an employment rate that much above the rate they actually have.

treatment.label: Physical health index at ages 70–74, evaluated through the employment–health relationship estimated on 50–54-year-olds

definition.value: Physical health index: the first principal component (converted to a percentile score, higher = better health) of the physical-health subset of the indicators — smoking, BMI, physical and mobility limitations, somatic diagnoses, visits to chiropractor and physiotherapist, and somatic inpatient and outpatient visits. In the second stage the index is evaluated at the older age group's own values and multiplied by the coefficient estimated on 50–54-year-olds.

timing.value: Measured at the SHARE interview, at ages 70–74; diagnoses and chronic illnesses over the 10 years before interview, healthcare utilisation in the year before interview.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity (physical health index)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = the counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) for the age group — the employment rate its members would have if the 50–54 employment–health relationship applied to their own health and characteristics — minus the age group's actual employment rate. Expressed as a share of the age group (the figure's y-axis is 'Employment rate', 0 to 1). The physical health index is the health measure used in both stages.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, at the SHARE interview; the age group is the individual's age group at interview, pooled over waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the age group (the y-axis of Fig. 3 is the employment rate, running 0.0 to 1.0); equivalently, percentage points of the employment rate divided by 100

magnitude.interpretation: The paper's own words: 'There exists considerable additional work capacity among the older individuals irrespective of which health index is applied' and 'The large additional work capacity is explained by a substantial reduction in the actual employment rate of individuals beyond 60 years of age.'

estimand.target_population: Danish women aged 70–74 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6) linked to the Danish administrative registers
estimand.formal_query: E[Ê_i^a | age group a] − E[E_i | age group a], where Ê_i^a is the employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) using the 50–54 coefficients

population.description: Danish women aged 70–74 in the Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, collected 2004–2015) linked to the Danish administrative registers; the prediction uses coefficients estimated on 50–54-year-olds of the same gender
population.selection: Danish part of SHARE (waves 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) respondents who could be linked to the Danish administrative registers; aged 50–79 with non-missing key variables including the personal identification number. identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation. The two-stage Cutler, Meara and Richards-Shubik (2013) health-capacity-to-work method: a covariate-adjusted employment–health gradient estimated on 50–54-year-olds (an age window not yet eligible for early retirement) is applied out of sample to the observed health and characteristics of the older age group, and the gap between that counterfactual employment rate and the actual one is reported as additional work capacity.

treatment.label: Education quartile (4th, highest, versus 1st, lowest)

definition.value: Additional work capacity = counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) minus the actual employment rate, by education quartile, gender, age group and health index.

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the estimation sample to ages 50–54 removes non-health-related retirement, because employment decisions at those ages are not influenced by the availability of early retirement; otherwise the estimated effect of health would be biased downwards.

claims.statement: Including a negative change in the health index between waves as a covariate leaves the estimated additional work capacity essentially unchanged: detriments in health do not significantly affect the capacity to work.

treatment.label: Negative change in the health index between SHARE waves (deterioration in health)

definition.value: The change in the health index between consecutive SHARE waves, entered as an additional covariate in the employment regression of Eq. (1); the paper examines the impact of a negative change (a deterioration) on the capacity to work. Sample sizes are reduced when it is included.

timing.value: Change between consecutive SHARE waves, i.e. roughly two to five years before the observation.

outcome.label: Estimated additional work capacity

definition.value: Additional work capacity = counterfactual employment rate predicted by Eq. (2) minus the actual employment rate.

timing.value: Cross-sectional, by five-year age group, pooled over SHARE waves (2004–2015).

units.value: share of the group (additional work capacity), compared with and without the change-in-health covariate

magnitude.interpretation: 'We find that the additional work capacity is similar for regressions that include a negative estimate of changes in the health index, suggesting that detriments in health do not significantly affect the capacity to work.' The authors add that the predicted employment rate is slightly smaller when negative changes in mental health are included, implying that mental health shocks do affect the capacity to work.

index_sets.over: individuals aged 50–54 in the linked SHARE–register sample

value.normalisation: H is the health index expressed as a percentile score (0–100) of the first principal component, a higher score meaning better health, so no omitted category applies to it; X contains education (4 dummies), married, born in Denmark, area of residence (4 dummies) and wave (5 dummies), each with an unnamed omitted category. Estimated separately for men and women.
value.link_function: identity (linear probability model)

value.claimed_domain: Other OECD countries with comparable healthcare systems — for the trends in predicted work capacity only; the authors say the magnitude of the additional health capacity to work may differ substantially across pension systems.
boundary_conditions: magnitude may differ substantially across pension systems (age at which citizens can retire, which disability pensions are available)
the estimates are averages and there is great individual variation; age does not dictate health status
the analyses are not normative and the estimates are upper bounds

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: This is somewhat surprising as others have found that acute health shocks greatly affect the probability of exiting the labour market (e.g., Trevisan & Zantomio 2016).

anchor_quote.text: We find that the additional work capacity is similar for regressions that include a negative estimate of changes in the health index, suggesting that detriments in health do not significantly affect the capacity to work.

extraction_notes: The main article contains no regression table: the digest lists five figures and no regressions. Every number in this extraction is either stated in the running text (footnote 3, the 10-percentage-point and 20-percentage-point comparisons) or measured off a figure against its printed axis, and each measurement carries a derivation record saying how.

Figures 4 and 5 and the self-employed/employee split are discussed in the text only by sign; the underlying numbers are in Additional file 1, which is not part of this PDF. Those claims carry a null point estimate with an absent record rather than a value read off a dense multi-panel figure.
Additional work capacity is a simulated counterfactual gap, not an estimated coefficient. It has no standard error anywhere in the paper and the authors describe it as an upper bound.
